questions.q: What does REPL stand for, and what is it for in Node?
options: Read-Eval-Print Loop, an interactive shell for quick experiments
Remote Execution Protocol Layer, a network tool
questions.explain: Typing node with no file opens the REPL, where each expression is evaluated and its result printed.

questions.q: Which command runs a file named hello.js with Node?
questions.explain: Pass the file path to the node binary.

questions.q: In the lesson's explanation, which engine does Node use to run JavaScript, and what is libuv for?
options: Chrome runs it; libuv draws the page
SpiderMonkey runs it; libuv compiles TypeScript
V8 runs the JavaScript; libuv provides the event loop, thread pool and non-blocking I/O
V8 provides the event loop; libuv parses code
questions.explain: Node is a C++ shell around V8 plus libuv; V8 runs pure JavaScript while Node adds I/O and timers.

questions.q: Why can the same hello.js run in Node and in a browser page?
options: It is the same JavaScript, as long as it avoids Node-only or browser-only APIs
Files ending in .js are converted automatically
questions.explain: The language is shared; APIs such as the DOM or file system are provided by the host environment.

questions.q: Which declaration should you prefer by default?
questions.explain: Use const by default, let when the value must change, and avoid var.

questions.q: What does typeof null return?
questions.explain: This is a famous long-standing JavaScript quirk.

questions.q: What is the result of 5 === "5"?
questions.explain: Strict equality checks type as well as value; loose == would coerce and return true.

questions.q: Which value is truthy?
questions.explain: The falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined and NaN; everything else is truthy.

questions.q: What does a do...while loop guarantee that a while loop does not?
options: The body runs at least once
questions.explain: do...while checks its condition after the body, so the body runs once even when the condition is false.

questions.q: Which loop is preferred for iterating over the values of an array?
questions.explain: for...of gives values; for...in gives keys or indexes and is mainly for objects.

questions.q: In a switch, what happens if a case has no break or return?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
questions.explain: Falling through is intentional when grouping cases such as "Sat" and "Sun".

questions.q: What does `continue` do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next
questions.explain: In the lesson it skips odd numbers; break is what exits the loop.

questions.q: What does a rest parameter such as ...numbers provide?
options: A real array containing the extra arguments
questions.explain: Rest parameters gather the remaining arguments into an actual array.

questions.q: What happens if you reference a let variable before its declaration?
questions.explain: let and const are hoisted but not initialized, so access before declaration throws.

questions.q: What does typeof a var variable return when read before its assignment line?
questions.explain: var is hoisted as a declaration only, so its value is undefined until the assignment runs.

questions.q: Which statement about arrow functions is true, according to the lesson?
options: They are always hoisted with their body
They must use the function keyword
They do not have their own this
questions.explain: Arrow functions offer shorter syntax and do not bind their own this.

questions.q: Which statement about map, filter and reduce is correct?
options: They mutate the original array in place
They return new arrays or values without mutating the original
questions.explain: Prefer them over manual loops for transformations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson write [...numbers].sort(...) instead of numbers.sort(...)?
options: sort cannot take a comparison function
sort mutates the array, so sorting a copy protects the original
questions.explain: Array.sort sorts in place; copying first leaves the original unchanged.

questions.q: What does nested.profile?.social?.twitter return when social is null?
questions.explain: Optional chaining short-circuits to undefined; adding ?? "none" supplies a fallback.

questions.q: How do you read the last element of an array with modern syntax?
questions.explain: at(-1) is cleaner than fruits[fruits.length - 1].

questions.q: What does `str.toUpperCase();` on its own line do to str?
options: Nothing to str; it returns a new string you must assign
questions.explain: Strings are immutable, so every modification returns a new string.

questions.q: Which syntax inserts a variable into a template literal?
questions.explain: Template literals use backticks and ${} for embedded expressions.

questions.q: What does "hello".startsWith("he") return?
questions.explain: startsWith tests whether the string begins with the given text.

questions.q: Which method pads a string on the left to a given width?
questions.explain: padStart(n) pads at the start; padEnd(n) pads at the end.

questions.q: Which method returns all elements matching a CSS selector?
questions.explain: querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of every match; querySelector returns only the first.

questions.q: What is event delegation?
options: Delaying an event with a timer
Attaching one listener to a parent and checking event.target for the child that was clicked
Attaching a listener to every child
questions.explain: It scales better, especially when children are added or removed dynamically.

questions.q: Which event fires as a user types in a form field?
questions.explain: input fires whenever the field's value changes; submit fires when the form is submitted.

questions.q: Why can't the DOM snippets run in Node.js?
options: Node.js has no DOM; they only apply in the browser
questions.explain: The DOM is provided by the browser, not by the JavaScript language or Node.

questions.q: What does a finally block do?
options: Runs only if an error occurs
Runs only if no error occurs
Runs whether or not an error was thrown, for cleanup
questions.explain: The lesson notes it always runs, no matter what.

questions.q: How do you raise your own error?
questions.explain: throw with an Error object, as in the withdraw example for insufficient funds.

questions.q: What does JSON.parse("not valid json") do?
options: Throws an error that a try/catch can handle
questions.explain: The catch block receives the error and can read error.message.

questions.q: Why is a bare catch that silently swallows everything a problem?
options: It hides bugs; you should inspect what you catch
questions.explain: JavaScript has no typed catch clauses, so check the error inside the block.

questions.q: How do you make Node treat .js files as ES modules?
questions.explain: Node treats .js files as CommonJS by default.

questions.q: How many default exports can an ES module file have?
questions.explain: A file may have many named exports but only one default export.

questions.q: What is package-lock.json for?
options: Pinning exact versions so installs are reproducible across machines
questions.explain: npm install records dependencies in package.json and exact versions in the lock file.

questions.q: What does npm run start do?
options: Runs the "start" script defined in package.json
questions.explain: npm scripts are named commands defined in package.json.

questions.q: Which browser feature does the to-do project use to keep tasks between visits?
questions.explain: The project combines DOM, events, error handling and localStorage persistence.

questions.q: Why does the project use event delegation on the task list?
options: Tasks are added and removed dynamically, so one parent listener handles clicks
questions.explain: One listener on the parent checking event.target works for children added later.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of the to-do app?
options: Add, mark done, and delete tasks
questions.explain: The app adds tasks from an input, lists them with status, marks them done and deletes them.

questions.q: Which Level 1 topics does the project combine?
options: Functions, arrays and objects, strings, DOM, events, error handling and localStorage
questions.explain: It is an end-to-end project tying together everything from Level 1.

questions.q: What is a closure?
options: A function combined with the lexical environment it was declared in
A block that closes a file
A copy of variables taken at call time
questions.explain: The inner function keeps a live reference to the outer variables, not a snapshot.

questions.q: In makeCounter, why can't you read counter.count directly?
options: count is private state held in the closure, not a property of the returned object
questions.explain: Only the returned methods can reach count; counter.count is undefined.

questions.q: counterA and counterB come from two calls to makeCounter(). Are their counts shared?
options: No, each call creates a brand-new independent count
questions.explain: Each call creates a separate closure, so counterA and counterB advance independently.

questions.q: What determines a function's scope chain?
options: Where it is written in the source, not where it is called from
questions.explain: JavaScript uses lexical scope.

questions.q: What does Object.create(animal) do?
options: Makes a new object whose prototype is animal
Copies animal's properties into a new object
questions.explain: The new object looks up missing properties on animal through its prototype.

questions.q: Why put methods on Person.prototype rather than inside the constructor?
options: Every instance shares one copy of the function in memory
questions.explain: ada.greet === grace.greet is true because both use the same prototype function.

questions.q: What does typeof Animal return for a class Animal?
questions.explain: class is syntactic sugar; classes are functions under the hood.

questions.q: In a subclass constructor, what must happen before using this?
questions.explain: super calls the parent constructor and must run before this is used.

questions.q: In the lesson's setTimeout(..., 0) example, when does the callback run?
options: After all synchronous code finishes, once the call stack is empty
questions.explain: Even with a delay of 0, the callback waits for the call stack to empty.

questions.q: What is a callback?
options: A function passed as an argument to be called later
questions.explain: Callbacks are often called after an operation such as a timer or request finishes.

questions.q: Which queue does the event loop fully drain before the task queue?
questions.explain: Promise callbacks and async/await continuations go into the microtask queue.

questions.q: What does the call stack do with function calls?
options: Pushes each call on and pops it off when it returns
questions.explain: JavaScript runs one thing at a time; each call waits for the ones it invokes to finish.

questions.q: Which are the three states of a Promise?
questions.explain: Once it settles (fulfilled or rejected) it never changes again.

questions.q: What does each .then return?
questions.explain: Chaining replaces the nested callback pyramid.

questions.q: What does an async function always return?
questions.explain: async/await is syntax sugar over Promises.

questions.q: What does await do inside an async function?
options: Pauses that function until the Promise settles, without blocking the rest of the program
questions.explain: Execution inside the function resumes once the awaited Promise settles.

questions.q: What does JSON.stringify do with a function-valued or undefined property?
questions.explain: Functions and undefined keys are silently dropped; null is preserved and Dates become ISO strings.

questions.q: Why wrap JSON.parse in try/catch for outside data?
options: It returns undefined for bad input
It throws a SyntaxError on invalid input
questions.explain: Data from a network response, user or file may be malformed.

questions.q: What does fetch return, and when does it resolve?
options: A Promise that resolves to a Response once the headers arrive; the body is read separately
A Promise that resolves after the body is fully parsed
questions.explain: You then call methods such as response.json(), which also returns a Promise.

questions.q: What does JSON.stringify(user, null, 2) produce?
options: A pretty-printed JSON string with 2-space indentation
A string with only two keys
questions.explain: The extra arguments handle filtering and pretty-printing.

questions.q: What does the g flag do?
options: Finds all matches, not just the first
questions.explain: The i flag ignores case; g finds every match.

questions.q: Which pattern matches exactly 5 digits across the whole string?
questions.explain: ^ and $ anchor to the start and end, and {5} requires exactly five repetitions.

questions.q: What does \w match?
options: A word character: letters, digits or underscore
questions.explain: \d is a digit, \s whitespace and . any character except a newline.

questions.q: How does exec() differ from test()?
options: exec returns match details (or null); test returns a boolean
test returns details; exec a boolean
questions.explain: With the g flag, exec can be called repeatedly to step through all matches.

questions.q: Why create custom Error subclasses?
options: So calling code can distinguish failure kinds by type instead of parsing messages
questions.explain: Subclasses like ValidationError can carry extra context such as a field.

questions.q: What does error instanceof ValidationError let a catch block do?
questions.explain: Branch on type, and re-throw errors you don't know how to handle.

questions.q: In the signup example, why does the catch block re-throw unknown errors?
options: It doesn't know how to handle them
questions.explain: Swallowing unknown errors would hide bugs.

questions.q: What does try/catch around await catch?
options: Both synchronous throws and rejected Promises
questions.explain: That is a main reason async/await is easier to reason about than raw .then() chains.

questions.q: Which file names does Jest look for by default?
questions.explain: Each test is a test() or it() call with a description and assertions.

questions.q: Which matcher checks deep equality of objects?
questions.explain: toBe is strict equality (===); toEqual compares objects and arrays deeply.

questions.q: What does describe do?
options: Groups related tests for readable output and shared setup
questions.explain: It organizes tests into named groups.

questions.q: How should you test async code in Jest?
options: Return or await the promise inside the test
questions.explain: Jest waits for the promise before deciding pass/fail, so async bugs aren't silently ignored.

questions.q: What does a bundler do?
options: Follows imports from an entry file and combines everything into a few output files
questions.explain: It resolves the dependency graph so the browser needn't make dozens of separate requests.

questions.q: What is tree-shaking?
options: Removing exported code that is never imported anywhere
questions.explain: Minifying strips whitespace and shortens names; tree-shaking drops unused exports.

questions.q: In "verify": "npm run lint && npm run test && npm run build", what happens if lint fails?
options: It stops at the first failure and does not run the rest
questions.explain: && only continues when the previous command succeeds.

questions.q: Which npm script names can run without the word run?
questions.explain: npm test and npm start are special shortcuts; others need npm run <name>.

questions.q: Which API does the weather dashboard project use, and does it need a key?
options: A paid API with a key
Open-Meteo, with no API key required
questions.explain: The project uses the free Open-Meteo API.

questions.q: Why does weather.js contain no DOM code or fetch calls?
options: So its data transformation can be unit tested with Jest without real network calls
questions.explain: A pure data-transformation module is easy to test.

questions.q: How should the app behave when the API fails?
options: Show a readable error instead of a blank page
questions.explain: Graceful failure handling is a stated requirement.

questions.q: Why do latitude and longitude default to London?
options: So the form works immediately without a geocoding step
questions.explain: The defaults remove the need for a geocoding lookup.

questions.q: What does Promise.all do if one promise rejects?
questions.explain: The other promises keep running, but their results are discarded.

questions.q: What does Promise.allSettled return?
options: The outcome of every promise, fulfilled or rejected, never short-circuiting
questions.explain: Use it when partial results are useful, such as checking which services are up.

questions.q: In loadDashboard, why is the total wait about 50ms rather than 80ms?
options: Both requests run concurrently via Promise.all
questions.explain: Concurrent execution takes as long as the slowest request.

questions.q: In what order does Promise.all return results?
options: The same order the promises were passed in
questions.explain: The array of results matches input order regardless of which finishes first.

questions.q: Which is true about require() and ES modules?
options: You can't require() an ES module, but ESM can import most CommonJS packages
require() can load any ES module
ESM cannot import CommonJS at all
questions.explain: The lesson's "mixing systems" section covers this.

questions.q: How do you get __dirname in an ES module?
options: Derive it from import.meta.url using fileURLToPath and dirname
questions.explain: __dirname and __filename exist only in CommonJS.

questions.q: Is the file extension required in ESM imports in Node?
questions.explain: In CommonJS the extension is optional; in ES modules it is required.

questions.q: Why was ESM introduced, per the lesson?
options: CommonJS require is synchronous and can be called anywhere, whereas ESM has stricter static import rules
questions.explain: require calls can happen conditionally anywhere in a file.

questions.q: What does app.use(express.json()) do?
options: Parses JSON request bodies into req.body
questions.explain: Without it, req.body would not hold the parsed JSON body.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code does the lesson return when a new note is created?
questions.explain: The POST route responds with res.status(201).json(note).

questions.q: For the route /notes/:id, how do you read the id?
questions.explain: Route params use req.params; query strings use req.query; JSON bodies use req.body.

questions.q: A client POSTs to /notes without a text field. What does the lesson's route return?
options: 400 with an error that text is required
questions.explain: The handler validates input and returns res.status(400).json({ error: "text is required" }).

questions.q: Why use prepared statements with ? placeholders?
options: They are the standard defense against SQL injection
questions.explain: Never build SQL strings from user input with template literals.

questions.q: What is true of better-sqlite3 according to the lesson?
options: It is synchronous, so no promises are needed
questions.explain: It is also very fast for typical app workloads.

questions.q: What does an in-memory array lack compared with SQLite?
options: It does not survive a restart
questions.explain: SQLite stores data in a file on disk, so it persists.

questions.q: How does MongoDB differ from SQLite in structure?
options: It is a file on disk only
Flexible documents (schema-optional) rather than fixed columns per table
questions.explain: MongoDB suits rapidly changing or nested data and uses a JSON-like query language.

questions.q: What is the goal of the module pattern?
options: Encapsulation: hide internal state and expose a small public interface
questions.explain: ES modules give file-level encapsulation, and closures give it within a file.

questions.q: What does a singleton guarantee?
options: Exactly one shared instance with a global access point
questions.explain: In the lesson, connectionA === connectionB is true for the database connection.

questions.q: Which four patterns does the module cover?
questions.explain: These are described as four of the most common patterns.

questions.q: In a module, why is a non-exported variable like count private?
options: It is unreachable from outside that file
questions.explain: Only exported functions can access or change it.

questions.q: What does TypeScript compile to?
questions.explain: Types only help catch mistakes before running the code.

questions.q: Why is unknown safer than any?
options: It must be narrowed (e.g. with typeof) before use
questions.explain: any disables type checking and should be a last resort.

questions.q: What does ? mean in isAdmin?: boolean?
questions.explain: Optional properties may be omitted without a compile error.

questions.q: What does an interface describe?
options: The shape of an object: required properties and their types
questions.explain: TypeScript checks that values used as that type match the shape.

questions.q: Why mock a dependency such as an email service in a test?
options: Real services cannot be called from Node
Mocks make code run in production
Tests stay fast and don't depend on network or external state
questions.explain: A mock replaces the real dependency with a fake version you control.

questions.q: What does jest.spyOn(logger, "info") do?
options: Wraps the method so you can assert on calls, optionally keeping the real behavior
questions.explain: Call mockRestore() afterward to restore the original implementation.

questions.q: Which assertion checks a mock was called with specific arguments?
questions.explain: toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) checks how many times it was called.

questions.q: What is supertest used for in this module?
options: Integration tests that exercise a real Express API
questions.explain: The module goes beyond unit tests to integration tests against an Express app.

questions.q: What is the first rule of performance work?
questions.explain: console.time gives quick rough timings; profilers show real bottlenecks.

questions.q: What does a memory leak mean in a Node process?
options: References to objects are kept alive unintentionally, so the garbage collector can't reclaim them
questions.explain: Memory grows over the process's life until it crashes.

questions.q: Which command lets Chrome DevTools attach for flame charts and heap snapshots?
questions.explain: Then open chrome://inspect and click inspect under Remote Target.

questions.q: What can high GC time in a profile signal?
options: Too many short-lived objects being allocated
questions.explain: It points to a memory-usage problem rather than a raw CPU one.

questions.q: What is the safe way to insert untrusted text into the page?
options: Set textContent, which is treated as plain text
questions.explain: textContent is never parsed as HTML, avoiding XSS.

questions.q: What does CSRF do?
options: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request they didn't intend, using their session cookie
questions.explain: For example, a hidden auto-submitting form on an attacker's page pointed at POST /transfer.

questions.q: In EJS, which tag is the dangerous unescaped one?
questions.explain: <%= escapes by default; the raw <%- helper on untrusted input is the danger.

questions.q: What does npm audit help with?
questions.explain: It is one of the practices covered alongside input sanitization.

questions.q: What does Vite use during development vs. production?
options: Native ES modules in development and Rollup for the production bundle
questions.explain: This gives instant startup in dev and an optimized bundle for production.

questions.q: Why use [contenthash] in webpack's output filename?
options: The hash changes when content changes, busting the browser cache
questions.explain: New content gets a new filename, so browsers fetch the update.

questions.q: What does the Vite server.proxy option for "/api" do?
options: Forwards API calls to a backend during dev
questions.explain: In the example it forwards to http://localhost:3000.

questions.q: What is code splitting for?
options: So users only download what a given page needs
questions.explain: It is one of the techniques that most affects real-world load performance.

questions.q: Why does the project use an in-memory database (:memory:) for tests?
options: Tests never touch catalog.db on disk while the same schema and logic are exercised
SQLite cannot use files in tests
questions.explain: A real file is used by the running app, :memory: by the tests.

questions.q: Which route updates an existing book?
questions.explain: The API offers full CRUD: list, get one, create, update and delete.

questions.q: What does the centralized error-handling middleware achieve?
options: Errors are handled in one place so nothing crashes the server
questions.explain: The project lists it as a requirement alongside validation.

questions.q: Which test libraries cover every route in the project?
questions.explain: The suite uses Jest with supertest against the Express app.

questions.q: In the layered architecture, which layer is the only one that knows about SQL or an ORM?
questions.explain: Routes handle HTTP, services hold business logic, and repositories handle data access.

questions.q: Why is the users service easy to unit test?
options: It depends on an abstract repository, so a fake can replace Postgres (dependency injection)
questions.explain: Business logic stays independent of HTTP and SQL.

questions.q: What is a monorepo?
options: Multiple related packages in one repository with one history
questions.explain: A polyrepo splits each package into its own repository; neither is universally right.

questions.q: What should controllers do in this structure?
options: Act as thin glue translating HTTP to service calls
questions.explain: The controller calls the service and maps results or errors to HTTP responses.

questions.q: What is the benefit of function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined over using any?
options: The return type is tied to the input type
questions.explain: first([1,2,3]) is number | undefined, while an any version loses type information.

questions.q: What does Partial<Product> produce?
options: A type with only required fields
A type where every field is optional
questions.explain: It is useful for PATCH-style update payloads.

questions.q: What does Omit<Product, "price"> produce?
questions.explain: Pick selects named fields; Omit removes them.

questions.q: What does <T extends HasId> do?
options: Restricts T to types that have an id
questions.explain: It is a generic constraint that guarantees a known shape.

questions.q: What is the most common microservices mistake?
options: Splitting by technical layer instead of business capability
questions.explain: Good boundaries are business capabilities, such as orders, inventory and notifications.

questions.q: What is a distributed monolith?
options: Services that can't deploy independently, combining microservices' operational cost with a monolith's coupling
questions.explain: If another team's release can block you, it isn't really an independent service.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of asynchronous messaging between services?
options: It decouples availability but adds eventual consistency
It removes the need for events
questions.explain: Synchronous HTTP/gRPC is simpler but couples availability.

questions.q: What does serverless mean in this lesson?
options: A cloud platform runs individual functions on demand
questions.explain: It is one of two paths when a monolith outgrows a single deployable unit.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authorization is login; authentication is permissions
Authentication verifies who you are; authorization decides what you may do
questions.explain: A valid token doesn't automatically mean the request should be allowed.

questions.q: Which status code does the lesson's requireRole return when the role doesn't match?
questions.explain: 401 is used for a missing or invalid token; 403 for lacking permission.

questions.q: Why are access tokens short-lived (15m)?
options: JWTs are hard to revoke early, so a short life limits exposure
questions.explain: A JWT can be verified without a database lookup, but can't easily be revoked before expiry.

questions.q: Where should the JWT signing secret come from?
questions.explain: The code reads process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET.

questions.q: What shape does the testing pyramid recommend?
options: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests and a small number of high-value E2E tests
questions.explain: Covering every click path would be slow and brittle.

questions.q: What can E2E tests catch that unit tests structurally cannot?
options: CSS hiding a button or a bug only in Safari
questions.explain: Playwright drives a real browser, so it sees rendered output.

questions.q: Which tool drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit in this lesson?
questions.explain: Cypress is mentioned as another E2E option.

questions.q: Why does the config set retries only when process.env.CI is set?
options: Flaky E2E tests get automatic retries in CI
questions.explain: retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0.

questions.q: What does CPU-heavy synchronous work do in Node?
options: Runs on a separate core automatically
Blocks the entire event loop and stalls every other request
questions.explain: Offload it to a worker thread to keep the event loop free.

questions.q: What does the cluster module do?
options: Forks multiple copies of the process, one per CPU core, sharing a port
questions.explain: A crashed worker doesn't take down the whole app.

questions.q: In the cluster example, what happens when a worker dies?
options: The primary logs it and forks a replacement
questions.explain: cluster.fork() keeps the pool at full strength.

questions.q: Why does Node handle many concurrent I/O requests well on one thread?
options: I/O such as database and HTTP calls is non-blocking
It uses a thread per request
questions.explain: Scaling beyond one core needs clustering, caching and load balancing.

questions.q: Why are WebSockets better than polling for live features?
options: One long-lived two-way connection pushes data the instant it's available
questions.explain: Polling wastes requests and adds latency equal to the interval.

questions.q: In the counter example, why does the server call broadcast?
options: To push the new value to every connected client, not just the sender
questions.explain: The server loops over all clients whose readyState is OPEN.

questions.q: What does Socket.IO add on top of WebSockets?
options: Fallback to HTTP long-polling and extras such as rooms
questions.explain: It falls back to long-polling when needed.

questions.q: Why does the server check client.readyState === client.OPEN before sending?
options: To avoid sending to connections that aren't open
questions.explain: Sending on closed sockets would fail.

questions.q: What is the main difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Delivery needs a human to approve the deploy; Deployment ships automatically on merge
questions.explain: Most teams use continuous delivery for production and full deployment for staging or preview.

questions.q: What does the matrix strategy in the test job do?
options: Runs tests against multiple Node versions (18, 20, 22)
questions.explain: It verifies the code on each supported Node version.

questions.q: What does needs: lint do on the test job?
options: The test job waits for the lint job to succeed first
questions.explain: Jobs form a lint → test → build → deploy chain.

questions.q: Why does the deploy job have if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'?
options: Only deploy from main, never from PR branches
questions.explain: The production environment can also require manual approval.

questions.q: Why use structured (JSON) logs instead of free-form text?
options: Log aggregators can filter and query them reliably
questions.explain: Examples of aggregators are Datadog, CloudWatch and Elastic.

questions.q: How does winston differ from pino in the lesson?
options: More configurable, with multiple transports, at the cost of more overhead
It only logs to a file
